item.title: Holiday Guidance for P.7 Candidates’ Parents
item.dc:creator: Bright Sparks Junior School
item.description: Our Primary Seven candidates have completed PLE, the first sat at our own UNEB centre, and started their long vacation. These weeks of waiting for results bring new freedom, and in today's hard economic times, new dangers: drugs, harmful social media, early relationships and idleness. The Head…
item.content:encoded:
Our Primary Seven candidates have completed their Primary Leaving Examinations and started their long vacation. This year carried special meaning for us: for the first time, Bright Sparks Junior School hosted its own candidates as a UNEB examination centre. We congratulate every candidate on their effort and thank parents for standing with us throughout the year.
The coming weeks, before results are released, are among the most delicate in a child's life. Our candidates are leaving childhood routines behind and stepping into adolescence. They suddenly have free time, less supervision and new curiosity, and the current economic hardship has left many parents working longer hours away from home. This combination exposes children to risks they have never faced before.
We therefore share this guidance so that, together, we protect the discipline, character and faith our children have built at Bright Sparks. Truly, we shall reach the shore but only if we row together.

The dangers our children face this holiday

Drugs and substance abuse. Drug and alcohol use among young people has spread into many neighbourhoods around Kampala and Wakiso. Children are often introduced to cigarettes, shisha, kuber, sachet alcohol, marijuana and energy-drink mixes by older friends, at video halls, bodaboda stages and late-night gatherings. Know who your child spends time with, know where they are, and watch for warning signs: unexplained money or items, red eyes, unusual smells, secrecy, sudden mood swings or loss of appetite.
Social media and online risks. A child with a smartphone and free time can be reached by strangers, pornography, online gambling and betting apps, cyberbullying and harmful "challenges." Many predators pose as young people to win a child's trust. Children should not hold accounts on platforms meant for older users, and should never share personal photos, location or family details online.
Inappropriate behaviour and early relationships. Idleness, peer pressure and unsupervised outings can lead to early relationships, sexual exploitation, teenage pregnancy and disrespect towards elders. Discuss these matters openly and calmly with your child. A child who can talk freely with a parent is far less likely to seek advice from the wrong people.
Pressures of the economic crisis. Hard times can push children towards quick money: hawking on the streets, gambling, running errands for strangers, or accepting gifts and "help" that come with conditions. Explain the family's situation honestly, teach the value of hard work and saving, and warn your child that no genuine adult offers money or gifts in exchange for secrecy.
Idleness. A child with nothing to do is the easiest target for all the risks above. A simple daily timetable ; chores, study, skills, play and rest, keeps the mind busy and the child safe.

Make the waiting period productive

Results will take some months. Use this time to build skills that will serve your child in secondary school and in life.
Learn a practical skill. Our pupils already practise liquid soap making, cookery, baking and ICT at school. Build on these at home, or introduce new ones:
  • Computer skills: typing, Microsoft Word, Excel and safe internet research
  • Cookery, baking and home management
  • Tailoring, knitting, hairdressing or crafts such as beadwork and mat weaving
  • Gardening, poultry or small-animal keeping
  • Music, drawing, drama and public speaking
  • A small home business, such as selling liquid soap or snacks, under your supervision
Read every day. Encourage at least one hour of reading daily: storybooks, novels, newspapers, the Bible or Qur'an, and early Senior One subjects. Ask your child to tell you about what they read, or write a short summary. Reading builds vocabulary, confidence and the independent study habit secondary school demands.
Limit screen time. Television, phones, tablets and video games should not fill the day. We recommend no more than two hours of recreational screen time per day, no screens during meals, and all devices out of the bedroom and switched off by 9:00 pm. Screens kept in shared family spaces are easier to supervise.

Keep them active through sport

Physical activity is one of the best protections against idleness, stress and bad company. Encourage your child to take part in active sports such as swimming, football, netball, athletics, basketball, volleyball, cycling, skipping and martial arts, as well as traditional games with siblings and neighbours.
Sport builds fitness, teamwork, discipline and self-esteem, and it tires the body in a healthy way so children sleep well. Where possible, enrol your child in a supervised holiday programme or club. For swimming in particular, ensure a qualified adult or lifeguard is always present  never allow children to swim in lakes, rivers, dams or unsupervised pools.
Uphold character and spiritual wellbeing
Our mission is to produce God-fearing, responsible citizens, and our core values  Discipline, Integrity, Excellence, Faith, Growth and Responsibility must not take a holiday. Parents are the first teachers of character.
  • Faith: Keep your child involved in prayers, church or mosque activities, Sunday school, madrasa and youth fellowships.
  • Responsibility: Assign daily household chores and hold your child accountable for completing them.
  • Respect: Insist on good manners, greetings, decent dressing and respect for elders and neighbours.
  • Family time: Eat together, talk together and listen. Praise good behaviour as readily as you correct mistakes.
Monitor phone usage. A phone gives the outside world direct access to your child, at any hour. We strongly advise parents to:
  1. Keep children on a shared family phone where possible, rather than a personal smartphone.
  2. Know all passwords and check messages, call logs, apps and browsing history regularly.
  3. Turn on parental controls (Google Family Link on Android, Screen Time on iPhone) and safe-search filters.
  4. Block or remove betting, dating and adult apps, and limit social media.
  5. Collect phones at night and keep them outside bedrooms.
  6. Explain why you are monitoring  out of love and protection, not suspicion so your child keeps talking to you.

Visiting relatives safely

Holidays are a good time for children to bond with grandparents and extended family. However, many cases of abuse and risky behaviour happen away from home, sometimes in the care of people the family trusts. When it is necessary for your child to travel or stay with relatives, please:
  • Know exactly where your child will stay, who will be in the home, and the sleeping arrangements.
  • Hand your child over personally, or use a trusted adult and reliable transport. Avoid sending children alone on bodabodas or long-distance taxis.
  • Agree with the host on clear rules: curfews, phone use, outings and the company the child keeps.
  • Make sure your child knows your phone number by heart and can call you at any time.
  • Call your child regularly, and speak with them privately, not only through the host.
  • Teach your child that their body belongs to them, that they may say "no" to anyone, and that they must report any person who makes them uncomfortable whoever that person is.
  • Bring your child home immediately if you sense anything is wrong.

While we wait for results

Waiting for PLE results can cause anxiety. Reassure your child that their effort is what matters and that your love does not depend on a grade. Avoid comparing them with other children. Use this time to plan calmly for Senior One together; school choices, requirements and the habits they will need.
The school will communicate the release of results and the next steps through official channels. Please rely only on information from the school or UNEB, and beware of anyone offering to "influence" results or admissions for money.

Let us row together

The holiday should be a time of rest, growth and joy not regret. With your close attention, our candidates will return from this break more skilled, more disciplined and closer to God and family. If you notice a problem or need advice, do not hesitate to contact the school.

Bright Sparks Junior School

A HISTORIC MILESTONE - OUR OWN PLE SITTING CENTER!

We are overjoyed to announce that for the first time since the establishment of Bright Sparks Junior School, our candidates are sitting their Primary Leaving Examinations (PLE) 2026 at our own UNEB Sitting Center, right here on our school premises!

After years of dedication, growth and hard work, our learners no longer have to walk to another center. They are writing their final exams in a familiar, calm and comfortable environment - at HOME.

This is a testament to the vision of our Director, the commitment of our staff, and the trust of our parents.

To our P7 Class of 2026, as you sit in our own hall, we are proud of you. Give it your best.

We Shall Reach The Shore!

item.title: BRIGHT SPARKS JUNIOR SCHOOL PREPARES FOR TERM III REOPENING AFTER A SUCCESSFUL TERM II
item.dc:creator: Bright Sparks Junior School
item.description: P.7 Candidates to report on 7th September, 2026 while all other continuing classes (KG-P6) are expected to report on 14th September, 2026
item.content:encoded:
SEGUKU, WAKISO   As Term II 2026 comes to an official close, Bright Sparks Junior School has announced comprehensive updates for all parents, guardians, and pupils regarding academic achievements, co-curricular developments, and key schedules for Term III.
In a school-wide circular issued by the Office of the Head Teacher, the administration expressed appreciation to the entire parent community for their trust and financial partnership, which allowed all institutional activities to run seamlessly throughout the term.

Academic Progress & Curriculum Coverage

Term II has seen strong academic performance and structured learning across all class levels:
  1. Candidate Class (P.7): Syllabuses across all subjects were fully completed. P.7 pupils wrote four comprehensive sets of Mock examinations (two internal assessments, WAPSSHA Mocks, and SUREKEY Examination Board Special Mock) followed by an intensive two-week remediation and concept clearance workshop.
  2. Continuing Classes (Kindergarten to P.6): Detailed progress reports have been compiled and issued. Parents are encouraged to review these reports with their children and support disciplined revision during the holiday break.

Co-Curricular Highlights & Educational Tours

Bright Sparks Junior School continued its commitment to holistic child development with significant achievements outside the classroom:
Wakiso District Primary Schools Ball Games: The school sports teams proudly represented Bright Sparks, competing up to the cluster level.
Academic & Clubs Exhibition Day: Held on Saturday, July 11, 2026, in the Main Dining Hall, the event featured project displays from various student clubs, entertainment by KTA, and delicious showcases from the Bakery Club.
Albertine Region Study Trip: Learners from Primary 5, Primary 6, and Primary 7 completed an enriching 4-day study trip to the Albertine Region, exploring geographical landmarks, ecological sites, and national oil exploration infrastructure.
Term III Reporting Schedule & Key Dates
To maximize candidate preparation while allowing continuing pupils adequate rest, the school has set a staggered opening schedule for Term III 2026:
DateEven/MilestoneTarget Group
7th September, 2026Early Reporting & Resumtion of ClassesP.7 Candidates
14th September, 2026Official Opening of Term IIIContinuing Classes (KG-P.6
26th September, 2026P.7 Leaver's PartyP.7 Candidates
24th October, 2026Academic DayAll Classes & Parents
30th-31st October, 2026P.7 Candidates' Dedication DayP.7 Candidates & Families

Financial Guidelines for Term III

School management reminds all parents that Term III is the final and briefest term of the academic year. A strict fee policy requires 100% clearance of school fees prior to learners accessing school premises. Parents with pending obligations are advised to engage the Bursar’s Office before the opening dates to ensure smooth entry and uninterrupted learning.
Head Teacher Muneeb Ali Wanyeni wished all Bright Sparks families a restful, safe, and productive holiday break as preparations continue for a successful Term III.

item.title: Tooro Mourns: Parliament Set for Special Tribute as Preparations Continue for King Oyo's Final Journey
item.dc:creator: Bright Sparks Junior School
item.description: A nation is in mourning. Across Tooro Kingdom and far beyond it, flags have been lowered, drums have fallen silent, and clans have gathered to grieve the passing of Rukirabasaija Omukama Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, the King of Tooro, who died on the evening of Thursday, 27 August 2026, at…
item.content:encoded:
A nation is in mourning. Across Tooro Kingdom and far beyond it, flags have been lowered, drums have fallen silent, and clans have gathered to grieve the passing of Rukirabasaija Omukama Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, the King of Tooro, who died on the evening of Thursday, 27 August 2026, at the age of 34 following a critical illness.
For most Ugandans alive today, King Oyo was the only Omukama of Tooro they had ever known. He came to the throne on 12 September 1995, a toddler of three years, after the sudden death of his father, Omukama Patrick David Matthew Kaboyo Olimi III, in August of that year. The image of a small boy seated on a throne far larger than himself travelled the world, and the Guinness World Records recognised him as the youngest reigning monarch on earth. He assumed the full duties of kingship at eighteen, in April 2010, and went on to reign for three decades.

Parliament to hold a special sitting

The Parliament of Uganda is today scheduled to hold a special sitting in the late King's honour. According to the Order Paper for the sitting, convened for the afternoon of 3 September 2026, a Motion for a Resolution of Parliament paying tribute to King Oyo is to be moved by the Prime Minister and Leader of Government Business, and seconded by the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Joel Ssenyonyi, alongside Members of Parliament from the Tooro sub-region, among them Mr Lawrence Akugizibwe, Ms Linda Irene and Ms Spellanza Muhenda Boguma. About seventy minutes have been set aside for debate.
The House had already paused to remember the monarch earlier in the week. On Tuesday, 1 September, the Speaker of Parliament, Mr Jacob Marksons Oboth, described the King's death as deeply painful and asked Members to stand with the people of Tooro in their grief. He told the House that when a king departs, it is not a family alone that mourns but a kingdom, a people and a nation. Members observed a moment of silence, and the Speaker signalled that a formal tribute motion would follow. Among the qualities repeatedly recalled in those remarks was the late King's interest in young people — his support for opportunities for the youth, and his use of international platforms to introduce Tooro and Uganda to the wider world.

Preparations for the return of the remains

Government and kingdom officials have been working jointly on the funeral programme. The Office of the President has confirmed that His Excellency the President will formally receive the body at Entebbe International Airport and pay his respects, after which the remains are to be flown onward to Kyegegwa District. From there, a slow road procession will carry the casket towards Fort Portal, allowing subjects along the route to bid farewell, before it reaches the Karuziika Palace, where a nine-day period of mourning is to be observed ahead of burial at the royal tombs. The Uganda People's Defence Forces are expected to render a gun salute as part of the official honours, and the President has directed that the late King be accorded an official burial with flags flown at half-mast.
Timings have shifted more than once as arrangements are finalised. Earlier announcements pointed to the remains arriving in the country on Thursday; the most recent reports indicate the return has moved to Friday. Readers are advised to follow official communications from the Tooro Kingdom and the Government of Uganda for confirmed times.

Clans gather, and questions of succession

At the heart of the traditional rites stands the Babiito royal clan, whose head, the Musuuga, oversees key cultural arrangements. The Kingdom's Prime Minister, Mr Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki, has assured subjects that the continuity of the Crown is secure and that the late King leaves an heir whose identity will be announced in accordance with Tooro custom. Consultations among elders and clan leaders are continuing, and some questions surrounding the succession are still being worked through by the Kingdom's own institutions. A condolence book has been opened at the Buziga Palace in Kampala, where mourners have been signing since last week.

A quiet lesson for our learners

For our pupils, this moment is more than a news headline. It is a living illustration of what they read about in Social Studies: that Uganda is a republic with an elected government, yet one in which traditional institutions such as Tooro, Buganda, Bunyoro and Busoga continue to carry deep cultural meaning; and that a cultural leader's authority rests not on political power but on the respect and identity of a people.
The Administration, staff and pupils of Bright Sparks Junior School join the rest of the country in extending heartfelt condolences to the Queen Mother, the royal family, the Babiito clan and all the people of Tooro.
We shall reach the shore.
Editor's note: This report is based on statements from the Parliament of Uganda, the Office of the President and Tooro Kingdom officials as reported in the national press up to 3 September 2026. Funeral arrangements remain subject to change.

item.title: NAMING OF UGANDA'S CRUDE OIL
item.dc:creator: Bright Sparks Junior School
item.description: In a historic gathering along the southeastern shores of Lake Albert, on 2nd September, 2026. President Yoweri Museveni officiated the unveiling and ceremonial naming of Uganda’s crude oil. The landmark event, hosted at the Kingfisher Development Area, brings the country a step closer to commercial…
item.content:encoded:
President Museveni Officiates Naming of Uganda’s Crude Oil as Commercial Production Approaches

KIKUUBE DISTRICT — In a historic gathering along the southeastern shores of Lake Albert, on 2nd September, 2026. President Yoweri Museveni officiated the unveiling and ceremonial naming of Uganda’s crude oil. The landmark event, hosted at the Kingfisher Development Area, brings the country a step closer to commercial petroleum extraction.

The project naming convention bridges Uganda's natural ecosystem with its national heritage. The flagship Tilenga project operated by TotalEnergies across the Buliisa and Nwoya districts—blends the Acholi word "Til" and the Runyoro/Rutooro word "Engabi", both referencing the native Uganda Kob and Bushbuck antelopes. Meanwhile, the Kingfisher field in Kikuube District, managed by CNOOC Uganda Limited, draws its title from the agile, fish-eating bird native to the Lake Albert basin.

Uganda’s petroleum reserves, estimated at 6.5 billion barrels in place with up to 1.7 billion recoverable barrels, present unique technical properties. Classified as medium-sweet crude due to its low sulfur content, the oil is exceptionally waxy, solidifying at room temperatures. To transport it from the Albertine Graben to the Tanzanian port of Tanga, developers are constructing the 1,443-kilometer East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP), set to become the world’s longest electrically heat-traced pipeline.

The government and joint-venture partners maintain that overall infrastructure including the Central Processing Facilities (CPFs) and well pads remains on track to achieve first commercial oil. Once fully operational, the joint developments at Tilenga and Kingfisher are projected to reach a peak extraction capacity of approximately 230,000 barrels per day.

Dear Parents and Guardians,

Warm greetings from the Administration of Bright Sparks Junior School.

As we approach the blessed occasion of Eid Al-Adha, I take this opportunity on behalf of the management, teaching, and non-teaching staff to extend our warmest wishes to you and your families.

Eid Al-Adha is a profound reminder of the values of devotion, obedience, and selflessness. As a school community, we greatly appreciate the sacrifices you make daily to ensure our children receive the best foundation for their future.

May this holy season bring immense blessings, peace, and joy to your homes. Let us use this time to reflect on unity, kindness, and charity within our community.

Please Note:

  • School will break for the Eid holiday to allow our families to celebrate together.
  • We kindly remind you to ensure our learners remain safe and find some time to engage in light revision during the break.

We wish you all a safe, peaceful, and wonderful Eid Al-Adha celebration!

Eid Mubarak!

Warm regards,

Muneeb Ali Wanyeni

Head Teacher

Bright Sparks Junior School, Seguku Katale
